# Sources {.unnumbered}

Every specific claim in this book — every date, dollar figure, name, address, and
quotation — is traceable to a source.

## How sourcing works in this book

Citations do not appear in the prose. This is a deliberate choice and it carries
an obligation, which is that the apparatus supporting the prose has to be real
and has to be inspectable.

It lives in three places.

The **bibliography** below lists the principal works the narrative was drafted
against, organised by act.

The **research log**, at `_project/research-log.md` in the manuscript
repository, records individual claims with their sources and a verification
status. It is the working document and it is where a fact-checker should start.

The **event ledger**, at Appendix B, gives the dated chronology with a status
against each entry.

## Standards

**Wikipedia appears nowhere in these sources.** It was used to navigate toward
primary and scholarly material, which is what is cited. That is a rule the
project set for itself at the outset and it has been kept.

**Contested claims are marked as contested.** Where historians genuinely
disagree, the text states the strongest version of each position, names the
uncertainty, and says which reading this book finds more persuasive and why. No
chapter's argument rests on a contested fact. The clearest instances are Jane
Stanford's death in Act II chapter 13, the doctrinal weight of the *Santa Clara*
headnote in Act II chapter 10, and the gesture at Capital One Arena in Act V
chapter 7.

**Figures carry dates and definitions.** Market shares, user numbers, and market
capitalisations move, and several of them depend entirely on how the category is
drawn. Where the book gives such a figure it states the date and the definition
in the text. Where a widely repeated figure turns out to originate in an estimate
rather than a disclosure — the frequently cited ChatGPT adoption number is the
clearest case — the text says so.

**Interested sources are labelled.** Several of the most detailed accounts of
events in this book were written by participants or by the institutions
involved: SRI's own history of the 1969 protests, Nike's corporate account of its
founding, a Stanford provost's memoir of the campus unrest, and Phil Knight's
memoir. These are cited as the positions of the parties that produced them, not
as the record.

## What is outstanding

This is a first complete draft and the apparatus is not finished.

Seven entries in the event ledger are marked `NEEDS SOURCE`, and the research log
carries a longer verification queue, weighted toward Act V where the inherited
drafts were richest in narrative and weakest in citation. Several claims carried
over from those drafts did not survive checking and were removed; the reasoning
is recorded at `_project/cut-material.md`.

The source tags `[S1]`–`[S87]` that accompanied the inherited event ledger
referred to a key that was not preserved. Rather than leave them as decoration or
invent a replacement, they have been removed and the ledger rebuilt with
verification statuses.
